standard.title: Geomorphological processes
standard.description: geomorphological processes that produce different landscapes and significant landforms
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain how water connects and changes places as it moves through environments (AC9HG7K01), and the causes and impacts of atmospheric/hydrological hazards (AC9HG7K04). They have not yet encountered tectonic, volcanic, or rock-weathering processes at this scale.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain geomorphological processes — including tectonics, volcanism, folding, faulting, weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition — that produce different landscapes and significant landforms.

nodes.label: Landscape diversity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the diversity of landscape types at the global and national scale, including wetlands, grasslands, forests, and deserts.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least three landscape types with one example location each.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe a range of landscape types (wetlands, grasslands, forests, hot and cold deserts) with national and international examples, explaining what distinguishes each type visually and environmentally.
wider: Compare landscape distributions across multiple continents, identifying climate–landscape relationships.
Examine how landscape classification systems differ (e.g., ecological vs geomorphological framings).
Investigate transition zones between landscape types and why boundaries are rarely sharp.
success_criteria: Identifies and names at least three distinct landscape types with a located example for each.
Describes at least one distinguishing feature that differentiates each landscape type.

nodes.label: Endogenic processes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how tectonics, volcanism, folding and faulting produce major landforms.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain one endogenic process (tectonic, volcanic, fold or fault) with a named landform example.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain how plate tectonics drives volcanism, folding and faulting, linking each process to a named landform example (e.g., MacDonnell Ranges — folding; Great Sumatran Fault — faulting; Krakatoa — volcanism).
wider: Compare landforms produced by convergent vs divergent plate boundaries.
Investigate how the same tectonic setting can produce different landform types (e.g., both mountains and rift valleys).
Examine how volcanic activity produces landscape diversity beyond just volcanic cones — lava plains, calderas, geothermal landscapes.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students conflate endogenic and exogenic processes, or treat all landforms as surface erosion products, they cannot accurately explain the formation of major landscapes in Node 3 or the hazard origins in AC9HG8K05.

response_modes.reason: Students need a clear conceptual model distinguishing internal (endogenic) from external (exogenic) forces before they can correctly attribute landform origins. A process-to-landform reasoning chain — plate boundary type → stress/movement → resulting structure — prevents conflation.

success_criteria: Names and explains at least two endogenic processes (e.g., folding, volcanism) and links each to a named landform.
Distinguishes endogenic processes (driven by internal Earth energy) from surface processes.

nodes.label: Weathering processes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how chemical and physical weathering break down rock to shape landforms, including the role of rock type.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain one type of chemical weathering and one type of physical weathering with a landform or landscape example.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain chemical weathering (oxidation, solution) and physical weathering (exfoliation, frost wedging), relating each to rock type (sedimentary, igneous, metamorphic) and a selected landform such as Fraser Island or the Twelve Apostles.
wider: Investigate how differential weathering rates between rock types produce distinctive landform features (e.g., tors, inselbergs).
Compare weathering processes in tropical vs arid climates and their contrasting landform outcomes.
Examine karst landscapes as a case study of chemical weathering at landscape scale.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding weathering as a prerequisite to erosion and deposition is needed for Node 4. Students who treat erosion as the only surface process will produce incomplete process chains when explaining landform formation.

response_modes.reason: Using multiple rock types and climate contexts helps students avoid exemplar lock-in where they treat sandstone + wind as the only weathering story. Breadth across rock types and climates builds a transferable process model.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Rock type–weathering interaction is a genuinely rich geographic concept — the same climate produces very different landforms depending on lithology. Wider students can explore how geologists 'read' landscapes through rock type, a transferable analytical skill.
success_criteria: Explains at least one chemical and one physical weathering process, identifying the conditions that drive each.
Links rock type to differential weathering outcomes in a named landscape or landform.

nodes.label: Erosion, transportation and deposition
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how erosion, transportation and deposition by water and wind shape landforms, using a selected local-scale example.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain how one agent (water or wind) erodes, transports and deposits material to shape a named landform.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the sequence of erosion → transportation → deposition by water and wind, applying this to a selected local-scale landform (e.g., Fraser Island formed by wind, waves and ocean currents; Twelve Apostles formed by coastal erosion and wave action).
wider: Compare the relative roles of water and wind as agents in landform formation in contrasting climate zones.
Investigate how human modifications (vegetation clearing, dams) alter natural erosion and deposition regimes.
Examine time scales — how the same processes that operate daily also explain large-scale landscape formation over geological time.

response_modes.reason: Applying the erosion–transportation–deposition sequence to multiple agents and settings (coastal, fluvial, aeolian) builds a versatile explanatory framework students will reuse when explaining hazards (K05) and human–landscape interconnections (K04).

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The ETD sequence (erosion–transportation–deposition) is a reusable conceptual tool. Wider engagement with multiple agents and scales equips students to apply this framework in novel contexts across the unit — including human impacts and hazards.
success_criteria: Describes the sequence of erosion, transportation and deposition by a named agent in relation to a specific landform.
Explains how the characteristics of the landform reflect the dominant process agent(s).

nodes.label: Process integration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how multiple geomorphological processes interact to produce landscapes, selecting and applying appropriate process explanations to named landforms at different scales.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the formation of one selected landform by identifying the dominant processes involved and how they interact.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain how endogenic and exogenic processes together produce a landscape or landform, applying process-based reasoning to examples at national and local scale. They distinguish between structural origins (tectonics, folding) and surface modification (weathering, erosion) in a coherent formation explanation.
wider: Compare two landforms formed by contrasting process combinations (e.g., volcanic island modified by weathering vs sedimentary landform shaped by erosion).
Investigate how the same process produces different outcomes in different contexts — e.g., water erosion in humid vs arid settings.
Explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples explain landform formation through Dreaming stories, considering what geographic knowledge these narratives encode.

response_modes.reason: Students need to coordinate process vocabulary and causal reasoning from Nodes 1–4 into a coherent formation explanation. The integration task — explaining a named landform using multiple processes — is where fragmented knowledge becomes geographic explanation.

success_criteria: Selects and names at least two geomorphological processes relevant to a chosen landform.
Explains how these processes interact or sequence to produce the landform's characteristics.
Locates the landform and identifies the scale at which the explanation operates.
